newsitem.title: CONGO: Fresh pre-election clashes in Congolese north.
newsitem.headline: Fresh pre-election clashes in Congolese north.

text.p: Four people have been killed in the latest clash between supporters of rival politicians in northern Congo, two days after party leaders meeting in Brazzaville pledged to avoid violence in the runup to next month's presidential election.

Shooting broke out on Monday as a convoy of vehicles belonging to former prime minister General Jacques Joachim Yhombi-Opango passed through Oyo, the home village of former president Denis Sassou Nguesso. Ten people were injured.
Twelve people were killed between May 7 and 11 in clashes in the northern town of Owando, in Yhombi-Opango's home region.
On Friday, the government banned private militias and the unauthorised carrying of arms, and on Saturday, party leaders pledged to avoid violence in any conflict arising from the July 27 election.

Political leaders signed a declaration at a meeting attended by Federico Mayor, director-general of the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organisation (UNESCO), and President Pascal Lissouba.
"Political parties formally and solemnly renounce the use of arms as a means of resolving political conflicts," it said.
Party leaders, who included Sassou Nguesso and opposition leader Bernard Kolelas, agreed to pass the message on to their supporters and to draw up an electoral code of conduct.
About a dozen candidates are expected to contest the elections. The three frontrunners are Lissouba, Sassou Nguesso and Kolelas, 1992 runner-up and mayor of Brazzaville.
Political parties armed their supporters during ethnic and political fighting following parliamentary elections in 1993 in which 2,000 people were killed in Brazzaville.
The militias were officially dissolved following a peace accord in 1995 but have continued to operate discreetly.

Followers of Lissouba and his ruling Panafrican Union for Social Democracy (UPADS) are known as "Zulus", followers of Kolelas and his Congolese Movement for Democracy and Integral Development (MCDDI) call themselves "Ninjas", and followers of Sassou Nguessou and his Congolese Labour Party (PCT), the former single party, are known as "Cobras".

Growing numbers of mainly Rwandan Hutu refugees have also fled to Congo from former Zaire following Laurent Kabila's takeover last month. The Brazzaville government is keen to repatriate them as soon as possible.
